The post was flagged as part of Facebook’s efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its News Feed. (Read more about our and Instagram.) Bankman-Fried founded the cryptocurrency exchange FTX in 2019, and it soon dominated the industry, as recently as January. FTX made headlines with a high-profile arena naming rights deal with the National Basketball Association’s Miami Heat, . It also had a 2022 featuring actor and comedian Larry David. But things came crashing down when the Bahamas-based FTX announced in a Nov. 11 that it was filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy amid of an $8 billion shortfall and a possible hacking. Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO, though he will stay with the company during its transition. Bankman-Fried has been a large donor to Democrats and left-leaning causes, but he’s also donated to Republicans, records show. Meanwhile, a Ukrainian official and the CEOs of companies involved in a Ukrainian cryptocurrency donation site dismissed the allegations in the social media posts as "nonsense" and "propaganda." Bankman-Fried’s donations Bankman-Fried Nov. 5 that he was a "significant donor" to both Democrats and Republicans in the primaries. Bankman-Fried that he and co-CEO Ryan Salame helped set up political campaigns to receive cryptocurrency donations, and gave millions of dollars to Senate and House Republicans. Federal Election Commission confirm that Bankman-Fried has donated money to candidates from both parties, although the bulk of his donations appeared to have gone to Democratic candidates and Democratic-leaning PACs in 2021 and 2022. That includes $27 million to the Protect Our Future PAC, which Democratic candidates and $6 million to the House Majority PAC, which . FEC reports show Bankman-Fried gave $45,000 to the and $105,000 to the Alabama Conservatives Fund, among others. What’s the Ukraine connection? A month after Russia invaded Ukraine, Ukraine launched Aid for Ukraine, a website where people from around the world could donate cryptocurrency to help Ukraine. A , the Ukraine’s vice prime minister and the nation’s minister of digital transformation, announced the site on March 14 described it as a "beautiful joint initiative" of the country’s Ministry of Digital Transformation "in partnership" with FTX and Everstake, a in Ukraine. let users earn rewards on their cryptocurrency deposits by committing them to a , according to CoinBase. The has a banner headline that reads "Help Ukraine with crypto, don’t leave us alone with the enemy." It said that it is powered by Everstake, FTX and KUNA. is a cryptocurrency exchange in Ukraine. The donation site’s URL in a move Aid for Ukraine said was developments. As of Nov. 15, Aid for Ukraine said it had raised more than $60 million. The bulk of that donor support appears to have been generated early in the conflict, according to . The money raised on the site is used to buy military and other equipment, according to a detailed listing of spending . A from Everstake announcing the partnership in March said "Aid For Ukraine is cooperating with the cryptocurrency exchange FTX which converts crypto funds received into fiat (government-issued currency) and sends the donations to the National Bank of Ukraine." Ukrainian and company officials rejected the claims that the nation then invested in FTX. , Ukraine’s deputy minister of digital transformation for IT development, Nov. 14 that claims Ukraine was funneling aid money back to Democrats in the U.S. are "nonsense." He said that the fundraising foundation used FTX to convert cryptocurrency donations to the country. "Ukraine's gov never invested any funds into FTX," he wrote. A fundraising crypto foundation used to convert crypto donations into fiat in March. Ukraine's gov never invested any funds into FTX. The whole narrative that Ukraine allegedly invested in FTX, who donated money to Democrats is nonsense, frankly 🤦‍♂️ — Alex Bornyakov (@abornyakov) , the founder of KUNA exchange, Nov. 13 that the Aid for Ukraine fund "used FTX in the first month of the war as an off ramp" to convert the cryptocurrency into Ukrainian money. "No crypto was stored on the FTX," he wrote. There is a lot of conspiracy around Aid For Ukraine Fund and FTX. We used FTX in the first month of the war as an off ramp to fiat in cases when we need fiat. No crypto was stored on the FTX. You can double check in chainanalysis. Remember, not your keys, not your crypto ✌️ — Michael Chobanian (@ChobanianMike) Everstake founder and CEO Sergii Vasylchuk also dismissed the allegations in a , suggesting it was Russian propaganda that was "spreading like a virus." 1/ Expecting Ukrainian to comment how FUD “Ukraine invested in FTX” is similar to expect to discuss russian narrative like “Ukraine invented military mosquitoes”. This is not a first, neither last info attack, which usually appears immediately after russians rekt on frontline — Sergey | Everstake 🇺🇦 (@sergattic) The press office for Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation responded to PolitiFact’s questions in an emailed statement. It described FTX’s role in the charitable effort as providing a "fiat off-ramp" for cryptocurrency sent by KUNA. The donations helped pay for Ukraine’s military needs, it said. FTX was not involved with the establishment, management of the fund or other processes, the press office statement said. All FTX-involved transactions took place in early March, the ministry said, and FTX’s involvement in Aid for Ukraine has ended. The ministry also said that $54 million of the money raised by Aid for Ukraine was spent on armed forces’ needs, and the remaining money is not stored at FTX. Nor has the Ukrainian government invested in FTX, it said. How much money has the U.S. sent Ukraine? Congress has approved about $68 billion in aid to Ukraine, according to Mark Cancian, senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. That money is mostly for weapons and military equipment, as well as emergency security and humanitarian aid, and includes in Ukraine-related aid approved in September. Cancian said "most of the (U.S.) aid goes through third parties and not directly to the Ukrainian government." "Much of the humanitarian assistance goes to relief organizations. Purchases of military supplies for Ukraine go to the contractor," he said. Cancian said it’s "not impossible" that money could be illegally diverted. However, he knew of no reports substantiating anything illicit had happened, and he was skeptical of the Instagram post’s claim. He said only a fraction of the U.S. aid has been spent so far, and that there are safeguards in place. "There’s no evidence that this has, in fact, happened," he said. Legislation passed by Congress about safeguards for transparency and accountability for cash transferred directly to the Ukrainian government. A State Department spokesperson said in a statement to PolitiFact that direct budget assistance to the Ukrainian government could not be used in the way that the social media posts suggest. "The direct budget support that the United States is providing to the Government of Ukraine is transmitted via a World Bank mechanism to Ukraine’s Ministry of Finance," the statement said. "There are agreements and monitoring mechanisms in place to ensure that U.S. funds are used for verified GOU expenses; the types of expenses for which U.S. funds can be used are specifically enumerated in those agreements." A spokesperson for the United States Agency for International Development told PolitiFact that the U.S. has given $8.5 billion in direct budget support to Ukraine’s government. That money was subject to World Bank safeguards and third-party monitoring and allowed Ukraine’s government to keep operating and respond to critical needs, such as keeping schools open and delivering healthcare.

statement: “Iran sentences 15,000 protesters to death.”
evidence: Stunning news out of Iran grabbed the attention of numerous celebrities and Canada’s prime minister. The only problem: it was wrong. "Iran sentences 15,000 protesters to death — as a ‘hard lesson’ for all rebels," read an that showed a photo of a woman holding an Iranian flag. Given Iran’s rights , the post’s statement seemed plausible to some. The post was including by celebrities including , Viola Davis and Sophie Turner. It even reached Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, who took to Twitter to the Iranian government over the development. Posts by Davis, Turner and Trudeau have since been removed. A Canadian government spokesperson told Trudeau’s tweet had been deleted because it "was informed by initial reporting that was incomplete and lacked necessary context." But posts like these were flagged as part of Instagram’s efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its News Feed. (Read more about , which owns Facebook and Instagram.) They appeared to have conflated three pieces of news. One, that an sentenced a protester to death because of charges of setting a government building on fire. Two, that the United Nations that as many as 14,000 protesters have been arrested in Iran over six weeks. And three, that most of Iran’s parliament has called on the judiciary to act decisively against the arrested protesters. So far, one protester has been sentenced to death in Iran — not 15,000. A Nov. 10 Newsweek may have inspired the initial confusion. It carried a headline that said, "Iran Protesters Refuse to Back Down as 15,000 Face Execution" and said the Iranian parliament had voted in favor of the death penalty for protesters. The story was Nov. 15 to note what fact-checkers : there was no indication such a mass execution was a certainty. "This article and headline were updated to remove the reference to the Iranian Parliament voting for death sentences," the correction read. "A majority of the parliament supported a letter to the judiciary calling for harsh punishments of protesters, which could include the death penalty." Protests broke out across Iran after 22-year-old Mahsa Amini died Sept. 16 while in police custody. The morality police had arrested Amini, a Kurdish-Iranian, for allegedly violating Iran's dress code by wearing her headscarf improperly. The Iranian government has that she died because of blows to her head, saying she died as a result of pre-existing medical conditions. In early November, Javaid Rehman, special rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran, said as many as 14,000 people had been arrested in Iran during the protests, . Estimates from Human Rights Activists News Agency, a nonprofit advocacy organization, put the number closer to 16,000 as of . On Nov. 6, 227 of Iran’s 290 parliamentarians called for the judiciary to consider severe punishments against the arrested protesters. "We, the representatives of this nation, ask all state officials, including the Judiciary, to treat those, who waged war (against the Islamic establishment) and attacked people’s life and property like the Daesh (terrorists), in a way that would serve as a good lesson in the shortest possible time," the officials said, according to from Iranian state media. However the parliament’s call is . Iran’s is in charge of sentencing. Experts from the United Nations the parliament’s decision, calling it a "blatant violation of the separation of powers" and urging "Iranian authorities to stop using the death penalty as a tool to squash protests." The U.N. experts said eight people have been charged with crimes carrying the death penalty: "waging war against God" or "moharebeh" and "corruption on earth." Other sources reported different numbers. Skylar Thompson, an advocacy coordinator of Human Rights Activists News Agency, told PolitiFact on Nov. 15 that nine arrested protesters face charges that could carry the death penalty. A Norway-based human rights nonprofit, , put the number at around 20. The international human rights group Amnesty International that in 2021, Iran had 314 death penalty executions, the second highest after China. As of July, Amnesty International put Iran’s 2022 figure at . Iran has instituted the death penalty in protest-related cases, giving people charged with these crimes limited access to lawyers and subjecting them to from authorities, according to Human Rights Watch, an international human rights group.

statement: Amazon’s Alexa confirms Michelle Obama “was born Michael LaVaughn Robinson.”
evidence: Do we need to fact-check Amazon’s Alexa? Though we’ve previously debunked claims that former first lady Michelle Obama is a who was born Michael LaVaughn Robinson, that former President Barack Obama as his "husband, Michael," and that this shows her as a man before they married, a video in a recent Instagram appears to show Alexa suggesting otherwise. "Alexa?" someone can be heard saying in the video. "Did Michelle Obama start out as Michael?" "Here’s something I found on the web," Alexa can be heard saying. "Michelle Obama, first lady of the United States, was born Michael LaVaughn Robinson in Chicago, Illinois, on Jan. 17, 1964." This post was flagged as part of Facebook’s efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its News Feed. (Read more about our ) We’ll say again: Michelle Obama wasn’t born Michael LaVaughn Robinson. She was born . Alexa also didn’t say as much when two PolitiFact staff members asked the same question in their homes. "Michelle Obama’s birth name is Michelle LaVaughn Robinson and she was born on Jan. 17, 1964," Alexa said in both cases. In 2018, Amazon that allowed users to create custom responses from Alexa. They could enter the the phrase they’d ask — like "What time should the kids go to bed?" — and then enter the answer they wanted Alexa to give, such as a bedtime for a babysitter. RELATED VIDEO Another custom Q&A example on Amazon’s "Alexa Skill Blueprints" : "Alexa, who is the best mom?" Alexa: "I just compared all moms in history and my conclusion is that yours is the best." We don’t know the backstory of the Alexa video in this Instagram post, but we do know that if you ask Alexa today whether Michelle Obama "started out as Michael," Alexa will correctly rebut the claim. And even if Alexa did give such a response, the claim itself is baseless. We rate claims that suggest otherwise Pants on Fire!

statement: No, the Pennsylvania Senate race wasn’t ‘rigged’
evidence: Declaring an election rigged does not make it so. A meme featuring President Joe Biden and U.S. Sen.-elect John Fetterman, D-Pa., suggests otherwise. Speech bubbles added to an image of both men make it look like Fetterman’s saying, "I can’t believe people actually voted for me." "They didn’t dumb ass," Biden replies. "Elections are rigged, geez." An Instagram sharing the meme was flagged as part of Facebook’s efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its News Feed. (Read more about our ) These, of course, are not real quotes, but we’re looking at the claim that Fetterman’s election was rigged. There’s no evidence to support the claim. According to unofficial election as of Nov. 15, Fetterman won with 51.01% of the vote. His Republican challenger, Dr. Mehmet Oz, took 46.57%. Oz the morning after Election Day. RELATED VIDEO We found no news reports or other credible sources suggesting evidence of widespread voter fraud in Pennsylvania’s election. We did see plenty of fact-checks debunking misinformation about the election, including some of our own. One debunked that an election results map proves the election there was rigged, and that Oz’s Instagram following, considerably larger than Fetterman’s, is proof the race was illegitimate. It’s not, and claims that the Pennsylvania election was rigged are baseless. We rate this post Pants on Fire!

statement: The death of a 4-year-old who appeared in vaccination campaign posters is linked to vaccines.
evidence: Social media posts are attempting to draw a connection between the COVID-19 vaccine and the death of a 4-year-old boy in Argentina because of his appearance in an advertising campaign encouraging vaccinations. Several Instagram posts have shared a screengrab of a from the conservative news website The Western Journal that read, "Poster boy for vaccination campaign dies suddenly at just 4 years old." Captions on the posts did not link to the full story and the boy’s death was linked to vaccinations, specifically the COVID-19 vaccine. One post shared Nov. 13 mentioning Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration. said, "We need a modern-day Nuremberg trial! What they did to these innocent children can not be overlooked." The posts’ claims appear to be based solely on the headline and not the article itself, which reported that the boy died of pneumonia. The Instagram posts were flagged as part of Instagram’s efforts to combat false news and misinformation on its News Feed. (Read more about , which owns Facebook and Instagram.) reported that Santino Godoy Blanco died Nov. 3 after coming down with a fever and being admitted to a local hospital. An autopsy determined Blanco died from bilateral pneumonia, which involves infection of . Blanco was featured in a from the Argentine Ministry of Health encouraging childhood vaccinations against measles, mumps, polio and rubella. The campaign was unrelated to the COVID-19 vaccine.
